source.author: lucan
source.text: Ferit amne citato Maliacas Sperchios aquas: et flumine puro Irrigat Amphrysos famulantis pascua Phoebi; Quique nec humentes nebulas, nec rore madentem Aera, nec tenues ventos suspirat, Anauros; Et quisquis pelago per se non cogntus amnis Peneo donavit aquas: it gurgite rapto Apidanos: nunquamque celer, nisi mixtus, Enipeus.
source.text_original: Ferit amne citato / Maliacas Sperchios aquas: et flumine puro / Irrigat Amphrysos famulantis pascua Phoebi; / Quique nec humentes nebulas, nec rore madentem / Aera, nec tenues ventos suspirat, Anauros; / Et quisquis pelago per se non cogntus amnis / Peneo donavit aquas: it gurgite rapto / Apidanos: nunquamque celer, nisi mixtus, Enipeus.
source.text_english: Spercheios, with its swift stream, beats the waters of Malis; and pure Amphrysos waters the pastures of serving Phoebus; and Anauros, which breathes out neither moist mists nor air wet with dew nor light winds; and whatever river, unknown in itself to the sea, has given its waters to Peneos: there is Apidanos in its swept-away flood, and Enipeus, swift only when mixed with others.

reuse.author: val
reuse.text: hinc laevom Telamon pelagus tenet, altior inde occupat Alcides aliud mare, cetera pubes dividitur: celer Asterion, quem matre cadentem Piresius gemino fovit pater amne Cometes, segnior Apidani vires ubi sentit Enipeus.
reuse.text_original: hinc laevom Telamon pelagus tenet, altior inde / occupat Alcides aliud mare, cetera pubes / dividitur: celer Asterion, quem matre cadentem / Piresius gemino fovit pater amne Cometes, / segnior Apidani vires ubi sentit Enipeus.
reuse.text_english: From here Telamon holds the sea to the left; from there Alcides occupies the other sea from a higher place. The rest of the young men are divided: swift Asterion, whom Piresius, his father, as he was falling, nourished with twin rivers, and slower Enipeus, where he feels the strength of the Apidanus.
